Q: What is the result of setting a variable equal to ISNULL in SQL? A:

The ISNULL() function lets you return an alternative value when an expression is NULL.

if @VARC is not null, @VarA = @VARC.

If @VARC is null, @VarA = @VarD.

Q: How to drop SQL default constraint without knowing its name? A:

Expanding on Mitch Wheat's code, the following script will generate the command to drop the constraint and dynamically execute it.

declare @schema_name sysname
declare @table_name sysname
declare @col_name sysname
declare @Command  nvarchar(1000)

set @schema_name = N'MySchema'
set @table_name = N'Department'
set @col_name = N'ModifiedDate'

select @Command = 'ALTER TABLE ' + QUOTENAME(@schema_name) + '.' + QUOTENAME(@table_name) + ' DROP CONSTRAINT ' + QUOTENAME(d.name)
 from sys.tables t
  join sys.default_constraints d on d.parent_object_id = t.object_id
  join sys.columns c on c.object_id = t.object_id and c.column_id = d.parent_column_id
 where t.name = @table_name
  and t.schema_id = schema_id(@schema_name)
  and c.name = @col_name

--print @Command

EXECUTE sys.sp_executesql @Command

Q: What's the difference between is_null($var) and ($var === null)? A:

There is no difference.

Besides, there are other expressions that check for multiple conditions one of which being test against null:

  • isset() checks if a variable is set or not null
  • empty() checks if a variable is not set or equal to null with loose comparison (e.g. 0, false, empty string, etc).

empty() and isset() do not trigger a PHP warning if their parameter is an undefined variable. In most cases, such a warning is desirable to pinpoint the bugs. So only use the functions if you believe your variable can be legitimately undefined. It normally happens with an array index.

✅ is true

❌ is false

⚠️ indicates a warning is triggered

isset($x) is_null($x) $x === null $x == null empty($x)
unset ❌ ✅ ⚠️ ✅ ⚠️ ✅ ⚠️ ✅
$x = null ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
$x = true ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
$x = false ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅
$x = 0 ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅
$x = 1 ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
$x = chr(0) ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
$x = "" ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅
$x = [] ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅

In summary (and to answer the question directly):

  • is_null($x) is equivalent to $x === null

Q: How to active a common profile according the property set in another profile? A:

The short answer is: You cannot.

If you have a look at the Build Profile documentation you can read the longer answer (emphasis mine):

The profile will activate if Maven detects a system property or CLI user property (a value which can be dereferenced within the POM by ${name}) of the corresponding name=value pair, and it matches the given value (if given). Since Maven 3.9.0 one can also evaluate the <packaging value> of the pom via property name packaging.

Simply put, a Maven Profile cannot be activated by property set within the POM itself. System properties are able to be used, as are properties defined within the settings.xml, but that won't help you here. A property within the POM simply can't activate a profile...and since profiles cannot set system properties or activate other profiles directly, this means profiles cannot activate other profiles.

The solution here depends very much on what you intend to do. You can use an explicit activeProfiles block in some modules, you can use files (like .mvn/active-profiles/integeration-tests), you can declare the property on the CLI. But you can't "chain" profiles this way, Maven simply won't allow it.
